name: Local and Air-Gapped Model Deployment
title: Local and Air-Gapped Model Deployment
answer: Local and air-gapped model deployment covers running language models, document review classifiers, and other AI systems entirely within a law firm's or legal department's own infrastructure, with no connection to external cloud services. It is used where client confidentiality, legal privilege, court protective orders, or data residency rules prohibit sending matter data to third parties. The scope includes model selection, hardware provisioning, software installation, data handling, and ongoing maintenance inside the secure perimeter. It also covers offline updates and patch management that must be brought in through controlled transfer points.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Local and air-gapped model deployment covers running language models, document review classifiers, and other AI systems entirely within a law firm's or legal department's own infrastructure, with no connection to external cloud services. It is used where client confidentiality, legal privilege, court protective orders, or data residency rules prohibit sending matter data to third parties. The scope includes model selection, hardware provisioning, software installation, data handling, and ongoing maintenance inside the secure perimeter. It also covers offline updates and patch management that must be brought in through controlled transfer points.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on dedicated servers or workstations with graphics processing units, high memory, and fast local storage, often housed in the firm's data center or a colocation facility. Air-gapped environments have no network route to the internet, so all model weights, code, and updates arrive on physical media or through a one-way data diode. Virtualization and container platforms are common to isolate models from other firm systems. Backup and logging infrastructure must also reside inside the boundary.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Teams typically start by inventorying the legal tasks that need AI support, such as privilege review, contract clause extraction, or deposition summarization. They then select an open-weight model or build a smaller fine-tuned model, transfer it into the isolated environment, and validate its outputs against a held-out set of matter documents. Prompting, retrieval augmented generation, and fine-tuning are all done locally, with no telemetry or usage data leaving the network. Quality control is manual at first, with lawyers reviewing model outputs before they are used in work product.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on model licenses, data provenance, and the duty to protect client confidences. Open-weight licenses vary in their commercial use terms, and a firm must record which model version and training data were used for each matter. Because the system is offline, audit logs, access controls, and version history must be maintained locally to show what the model saw and produced. Risk assessments cover hardware failure, insider access, stale models, and the inability to receive automatic security patches.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Local and air-gapped deployment is moving toward smaller, more efficient models that can run on a single secure workstation rather than a rack of servers. Legal teams are likely to see more packaged, offline-ready tools with built-in logging and e-discovery integrations. Hardware costs are falling while open-weight model quality improves, making isolated deployment practical for mid-size firms. The main open question is how courts and regulators will treat locally deployed models in discovery and privilege disputes, especially when a model's training data or fine-tuning set is itself subject to challenge.
